incidents.root_cause_detail: Outbound pool exhausted when a burst of merchant requests occupied PSP sessions faster than they were released; MC_POOL_WAIT accompanied rising acquisition waits.
incidents.response: Responders separated inbound queue growth from active outbound calls, reduced admission temporarily, and let occupied sessions drain before restoring normal intake.
incidents.boundary: The failure involved outbound provider capacity rather than a database pool. This report does not establish a general policy for increasing the configured ceiling.

incidents.root_cause_detail: PSP sessions were consumed by excess worker fan-out introduced in a concurrency configuration deployment. The resulting capacity pressure outlasted individual client timeouts.
incidents.response: Operators compared worker admission with the release baseline, reverted the fan-out adjustment, and observed the waiting queue drain while retaining request references for reconciliation.
incidents.boundary: The preceding change is part of the confirmed event sequence. A timeout still did not establish whether every affected business instruction had failed permanently.

incidents.root_cause_detail: MerchantConnect client pool starvation was amplified by retries after a worker retry-timing deployment. Retried attempts competed with original calls for the same outbound sessions.
incidents.response: The team compared attempts per request with active sessions, reverted the retry-timing change, and constrained intake during recovery. Investigation retained both original and retry attempt identifiers.
incidents.boundary: The root-cause family is capacity because exhaustion of outbound sessions interrupted service. The presence of retries does not make this a duplicate-debit incident.

incidents.root_cause_detail: Slow PSP responses held MerchantConnect outbound connections while new merchant requests continued to arrive. Acquisition waits increased until callers observed timeouts.
incidents.response: Responders verified that workers were available, identified occupied PSP sessions as the constrained resource, and reduced incoming work while the dependency recovered.
incidents.boundary: This event concerned capacity held by slow responses, not an observed provider connection reset. Similar client errors alone are insufficient to merge those mechanisms.

incidents.root_cause_detail: MerchantConnect outbound pool exhaustion recurred as requests continued entering a saturated downstream path. Waiting work triggered further attempts and prolonged pressure on the client pool.
incidents.response: Operators captured pool-acquisition waits and repeated request references, contained admission, and preserved queue observations for a subsequent tuning review.
incidents.boundary: Restoration of the queue did not demonstrate removal of the feedback loop. Follow-up remediation required its own implementation and operating evidence.

incidents.root_cause_detail: Unbounded concurrency and retry amplification starved MerchantConnect outbound sessions. MC_POOL_WAIT appeared with waiting requests even though inbound workers remained available.
incidents.response: Responders reduced admission, preserved attempt-to-request relationships, and observed recovery as occupied sessions drained. The report recommended architectural examination of the repeated feedback loop.
incidents.boundary: The available event evidence supports a mechanism investigation. A later meeting proposal or architecture decision must not be treated as already approved at this report's publication.

incidents.root_cause_detail: A short merchant burst exhausted the bounded outbound allocation before back pressure stabilized admission. A minor capacity interruption remained visible after the July control rollout.
incidents.response: The responder inspected admission limits, circuit state, and retry-budget use, then allowed the constrained queue to drain without treating the new controls as permission to expand capacity automatically.
incidents.boundary: The event is retained as an observed residual failure. It does not establish that the rollout had no benefit, and it prevents a claim that capacity incidents were eliminated.

incidents.root_cause_detail: PayFlow checkout workers exhausted their outbound MerchantConnect allocation during a concentrated traffic burst. The constrained resource was the outbound request pool, not PayFlow's database connection pool.
incidents.response: Responders separated outbound waiting from database acquisition metrics, limited checkout admission, and preserved pending outcomes for status reconciliation.
incidents.boundary: This is a PayFlow capacity event. It should not be counted as a MerchantConnect-owned capacity incident merely because MerchantConnect was the downstream dependency.

incidents.root_cause_detail: A PayFlow retry worker lost a lease acknowledgement and scheduled an already-pending status attempt again. Repeated retries consumed the operation's permitted attempt budget.
incidents.response: The response suspended the affected retry path, reconciled pending status references, and restarted work only after distinguishing original operations from repeated attempts.
incidents.boundary: The reviewed defect is in retry scheduling. The event does not record executed duplicate debits or evidence that a merchant idempotency boundary was absent.

incidents.root_cause_detail: A MerchantConnect deployment reset retry counters when work moved between workers. Operations consequently exceeded the intended retry allowance and received downstream rejections.
incidents.response: Operators compared retry counters across worker handoff, reverted the affected release, and reconciled outstanding request identifiers before resuming normal retries.
incidents.boundary: This retry-budget defect is separate from the later missing-key payment boundary. Shared family membership is not proof of an identical cause.

incidents.root_cause_detail: A PayFlow retry-jitter deployment synchronized delayed attempts instead of dispersing them. Concentrated retry traffic caused requests to exhaust their permitted processing window.
incidents.response: Responders compared retry timestamps across pending work, reverted the scheduling change, and observed recovery while preserving the original business operation references.
incidents.boundary: The event records failed or rejected attempts, not a count of unique customers. It does not quantify the monetary effect of those attempts.

incidents.root_cause_detail: Retries crossed the MerchantConnect payment boundary without a merchant-scoped idempotency key after the July retry redesign. Interrupted acknowledgements could trigger independent execution, and duplicate debits were observed.
incidents.response: The response contained the affected retry path and reconciled business instructions with settlement references. Investigators separated repeated network attempts from independently executed debits rather than treating the error counter as a duplicate count.
incidents.boundary: The 44,700 failed or rejected attempts are not the number of duplicate debits. The report does not record an exact currency loss or establish that every retry-family event shares this mechanism.

incidents.root_cause_detail: A PayFlow deployment changed retry classification so terminal declines re-entered the retry queue. Repeatedly attempting a terminal outcome consumed processing capacity and generated further rejections.
incidents.response: Operators restored the previous classification behavior, removed confirmed terminal outcomes from the retry path, and reconciled ambiguous requests separately.
incidents.boundary: This is a retry classification defect, not evidence of missing merchant-scoped keys in MerchantConnect. A terminal decline must not be retried merely to seek a different answer.

incidents.root_cause_detail: A MerchantConnect worker-lease deployment prematurely released retry ownership during acknowledgement reconciliation. Multiple workers attempted the same reconciliation task, producing rejected attempts and delayed resolution.
incidents.response: The team reverted the lease change and restored single ownership of pending reconciliation tasks. Persisted operation records were retained while outstanding outcomes were resolved.
incidents.boundary: The reviewed defect concerns reconciliation ownership after the duplicate-prevention release. This report does not record renewed duplicate debits or universal failure of the idempotency fix.

incidents.root_cause_detail: The PSP Gateway received provider-side connection resets, recorded as PSP_CONN_RESET. The upstream session was closed before a complete response reached the gateway.
incidents.response: Operators confirmed the failure boundary using reset observations, limited repeated calls to the provider, and reconciled uncertain outcomes after the external path recovered.
incidents.boundary: A connection reset is not the same as local pool exhaustion. The external dependency interruption explains this event without establishing the provider's internal root cause.

incidents.root_cause_detail: An external PSP accepted connections but responded slowly enough that MerchantConnect requests exceeded their processing window. The provider degradation persisted after local worker availability was confirmed.
incidents.response: The incident response reduced repeated calls, retained unresolved operation references, and waited for verified provider recovery before returning to normal throughput.
incidents.boundary: Although MerchantConnect was affected, the confirmed family is external PSP degradation. Counting every merchant timeout as local capacity exhaustion would misclassify the event.

incidents.root_cause_detail: The PSP Gateway experienced prolonged upstream response unavailability. Local request handling remained available, but the external authorization path did not provide usable responses.
incidents.response: Responders checked the boundary between local acceptance and upstream completion, suppressed unnecessary retries, and reconciled uncertain authorization references after recovery.
incidents.boundary: The report establishes an external service interruption as observed by Northstar. It does not speculate about an unobserved internal failure at the fictional provider.

incidents.root_cause_detail: MerchantConnect encountered intermittent upstream authorization errors during an external PSP degradation. Retrying the same operation did not reliably obtain a final response.
incidents.response: Operators preserved the original operation references, limited repeated provider calls, and used post-recovery reconciliation to distinguish rejected attempts from completed payments.
incidents.boundary: The event's duration is the attributable interruption interval. It is not a measurement of the provider's entire outage across all of its customers.

incidents.root_cause_detail: Provider-side throttling interrupted PSP Gateway authorization attempts. Local capacity was available, but upstream rejection prevented successful completion of the affected requests.
incidents.response: The response confirmed the remote rejection boundary, constrained request pressure, and resumed ordinary traffic only after successful responses returned consistently.
incidents.boundary: The report classifies observed external degradation. It does not infer that changing Northstar's local connection ceiling would have removed the provider's restriction.

incidents.root_cause_detail: SettlementHub consumer lag accumulated behind an EventMesh event burst. Accepted payment work reached downstream reconciliation later than expected.
incidents.response: Operators compared event timestamps with committed consumer position, paced recovery to the downstream reconciliation path, and retained the delayed event references.
incidents.boundary: A payment's acceptance time and appearance in a report are different milestones. This event does not establish a ledger posting-order defect.

incidents.root_cause_detail: A stalled SettlementHub consumer partition left an increasing age of unprocessed events while other partitions continued. Aggregate process availability obscured the delayed subset.
incidents.response: The responder examined partition progress, restored the stalled consumer path, and verified reconciliation of outstanding events before advancing the reporting cutoff.
incidents.boundary: A running consumer group alone would have overstated recovery. The report concerns event backlog, not a confirmed financial loss from delayed reporting.

incidents.root_cause_detail: A campaign spike reached SettlementHub after a consumer configuration change had reduced effective processing capacity. EventMesh lag delayed settlement consumption and reconciliation.
incidents.response: The response compared consumer progress against the campaign window, restored the preceding consumer setting, and drained outstanding events while preserving downstream ordering.
incidents.boundary: The observed backlog supports a change-related event. Its effect on corporate reporting requires the downstream product and architecture evidence rather than an assumed universal customer impact.

incidents.root_cause_detail: A concentrated settlement batch exceeded the bounded consumption path's short-term processing allowance. Event age increased until the batch could be reconciled.
incidents.response: Responders watched event age and downstream acknowledgements together, paced catch-up, and advanced the report cutoff only after outstanding work completed.
incidents.boundary: A bounded recovery mechanism can coexist with a later backlog event. This report does not establish that the prior consumer change was absent or ineffective in every condition.

incidents.root_cause_detail: PayFlow database connection-pool waits grew behind long-running transaction locks. PF_DB_POOL_WAIT identified the database acquisition boundary rather than the outbound PSP client pool.
incidents.response: Operators identified the blocking transaction path, constrained competing work, and restored database access while retaining request outcomes for reconciliation.
incidents.boundary: The word pool is a lexical similarity to MerchantConnect incidents, but the constrained resource and root-cause family are different.

incidents.root_cause_detail: A SettlementHub database-index deployment increased lock contention during reconciliation writes. The resulting database waits delayed processing of otherwise available settlement work.
incidents.response: The response compared write latency with the release baseline, reverted the index change, and reconciled outstanding work after locks cleared.
incidents.boundary: The event is database contention associated with a change. It must not be relabeled as EventMesh backlog solely because settlement completion was delayed.

incidents.root_cause_detail: PayFlow hot-row contention serialized checkout state updates under concentrated access. Database waits increased while outbound payment capacity remained available.
incidents.response: Responders reduced competing updates to the affected state path, preserved pending operation identifiers, and observed recovery after the blocking pressure subsided.
incidents.boundary: The confirmed mechanism concerns local database serialization. A client timeout by itself would not distinguish this from an outbound provider problem.

incidents.root_cause_detail: MerchantConnect resolver timeouts prevented establishment of new PSP connections. Existing sessions and worker capacity did not remove the need to resolve the upstream endpoint.
incidents.response: Responders verified resolution separately from connection acquisition, restored the resolver path, and reconciled requests that had timed out before connection establishment.
incidents.boundary: This is a MerchantConnect DNS event, not an outbound-capacity event. Counting it with pool starvation would conflate failure to locate an endpoint with lack of available sessions.

incidents.root_cause_detail: A PSP Gateway routing deployment directed authorization traffic through an unavailable network path. Requests failed before a usable provider response could return.
incidents.response: The response compared route configuration with the preceding baseline, reverted the routing change, and confirmed successful connections before reopening ordinary admission.
incidents.boundary: The change relation is supported by route evidence. It does not establish provider-side degradation or a failure of the idempotency contract.

incidents.root_cause_detail: MerchantConnect trust configuration rejected the provider certificate chain during connection establishment. TLS_TRUST_FAILURE was retained with affected request references.
incidents.response: Operators verified the certificate boundary, restored the approved trust configuration, and reconciled operations whose attempts had failed before a usable session formed.
incidents.boundary: This is a certificate or configuration event. It does not imply that the fictional provider's certificate was malicious or that a local capacity change was warranted.

incidents.root_cause_detail: A PayFlow deployment supplied an invalid timeout configuration to the outbound request path. Requests expired before the expected response interval could complete.
incidents.response: The team compared the effective setting with the release baseline, reverted the configuration change, and checked recovery through the customer-visible status path.
incidents.boundary: The failure belongs to configuration, despite timeout symptoms. It does not prove a repeated MerchantConnect capacity mechanism.

incidents.root_cause_detail: An expired AuthHub certificate interrupted authentication. AUTH_TLS_EXPIRED identified the certificate boundary and an alert-routing gap delayed recognition by the responsible responder.
incidents.response: The team restored the approved certificate and checked authentication recovery separately from alert routing. Follow-up work retained the ownership gap as a distinct action.
incidents.boundary: The event concerns authentication infrastructure. Its impact belongs to the identity service and cannot establish present certificate or employee status.

incidents.root_cause_detail: AuthHub HTTP client pool starvation affected identity lookups. AUTH_HTTP_POOL_WAIT used wording similar to payment connection failures but referred to the authentication client boundary.
incidents.response: Responders identified the identity lookup dependency, constrained concurrent requests, and allowed occupied HTTP sessions to drain before resuming normal admission.
incidents.boundary: This event concerns the identity lookup boundary. Shared pool terminology does not make it an interruption of the merchant payment service.

incidents.root_cause_detail: A regional DR exercise restored the database but left NotifyHub unavailable through the exercised recovery path. The exercise inventory had omitted the notification dependency.
incidents.response: Responders recorded successful database checks and failed notification delivery separately. Customer-visible notification remained partial, and the dependency omission was referred for architectural review.
incidents.boundary: The duration measures the exercise's attributable notification interruption. It is not a current regional-health observation or a payment-outage interval.

incidents.root_cause_detail: A cohort-mapping configuration defect after MODEL-2026-04 caused inappropriate review routing and a customer-visible false-positive spike. The incident captures a specific operational symptom within the broader model-governance story.
incidents.response: Risk-authorized responders corrected the mapping, retained decision samples, and reviewed affected dispositions without disclosing feature values in customer messages.
incidents.boundary: This configuration event does not establish a measured fraud loss or prove that the previously approved bounded threshold adjustment was never implemented.

incidents.root_cause_detail: A LedgerCore posting-order race produced inconsistent reconciliation order and required a manual accounting adjustment. The failure was inside the posting path rather than the EventMesh consumer boundary.
incidents.response: The team contained competing posting work, reconciled affected entry references, and retained the adjustment rationale for an independent control review.
incidents.boundary: The event concerns the finance posting path. A broader payment analysis must state whether that path is in scope rather than silently treating every reconciliation event as a merchant payment interruption.

incidents.root_cause_detail: DataGateway resolver timeouts interrupted its own upstream lookup path. DG_DNS_TIMEOUT described name resolution rather than occupied MerchantConnect PSP sessions.
incidents.response: Responders verified resolver behavior, restored the lookup path, and retained the affected service identity with the original error observations.
incidents.boundary: This event is unrelated to MerchantConnect capacity recurrence. The existence of a dependency relationship is insufficient to assert that the same incident propagated into payments.

documents.title: Bounded concurrency and back pressure decision

sections.heading: Design position
sections.text: The architecture forum approves bounded concurrency, back pressure, circuit breaking, and retry budgets for MerchantConnect. Doubling the outbound connection pool alone is rejected as the durable solution because it does not bound retry amplification.

sections.heading: Supporting detail
sections.text: Admission must stop adding work when the downstream budget is exhausted. Circuit state must suppress calls to an unhealthy dependency, and retries must consume an explicit budget. The design preserves correlation identifiers so operators can follow one request through every attempted delivery.

sections.heading: Scope and interpretation
sections.text: Acceptance of the design is separate from deployment and change approval. A larger pool may be a temporary mitigation under the applicable control process, but is not the architecture decision recorded here.

sections.heading: Business and service context
sections.text: Merchant payment processing crosses an outbound provider boundary. Waiting work, active connections, and client-visible responses describe different parts of that journey. A useful investigation preserves those distinctions and relates observations to the particular configuration and procedure in force. A temporary reduction in waiting work can be operationally useful without explaining why the original pressure accumulated. Service identity and observation time therefore remain essential when comparing records that use similar words for different failure modes.

sections.heading: Review method
sections.text: Read the interface boundary and assumptions before applying the design to an incident. Compare the behavior described here with the configuration and procedure effective for the event under examination. Record which observations support the mechanism and which remain hypotheses. A design or accepted decision can explain intended behavior, but implementation and operating evidence must be inspected separately when the question concerns what actually occurred.

sections.heading: Design position
sections.text: The payment architecture forum mandates merchant-scoped idempotency keys and replay-safe settlement. A repeated request with the same merchant and key must resolve against the recorded operation rather than initiate an independent debit.

sections.heading: Supporting detail
sections.text: The key is bound to the normalized request payload. Reuse with a different payload must fail explicitly; ambiguous settlement acknowledgements must be reconciled before another submission. Persistence of the result must survive a worker restart so retries cannot bypass the boundary.

sections.heading: Scope and interpretation
sections.text: This decision specifies the target behavior. Evidence that a release was deployed belongs in the change record; evidence of the version running today requires the deployment system.

sections.heading: Business and service context
sections.text: A payment operation can produce several network attempts. The commercial instruction, the transport attempt, and the settlement entry must remain distinguishable throughout investigation. An interrupted acknowledgement leaves uncertainty about the operation's result; it does not establish that repeating the request is harmless. Interface contracts and persistence boundaries determine what a retry means. Evidence should connect these boundaries through stable references before an analyst classifies an apparent duplicate or recommends further processing.

sections.heading: Review method
sections.text: Read the interface boundary and assumptions before applying the design to an incident. Compare the behavior described here with the configuration and procedure effective for the event under examination. Record which observations support the mechanism and which remain hypotheses. A design or accepted decision can explain intended behavior, but implementation and operating evidence must be inspected separately when the question concerns what actually occurred.

sections.heading: Application example
sections.text: For example, a worker can submit a payment and lose the acknowledgement before returning a response to the merchant. The next worker must consult the same operation record before deciding what to do. It must not infer that the first submission failed merely because the first worker is no longer available. If the settlement outcome remains ambiguous, reconciliation is part of completing the operation, rather than a reason to create a second independent instruction.

sections.heading: Design position
sections.text: The messaging architecture decision adopts bounded event consumption with explicit backlog management. Settlement consumers must report event age and committed position rather than presenting a running process as proof that processing has caught up.

sections.heading: Supporting detail
sections.text: Recovery prioritizes safe acknowledgement and reconciliation of outstanding work. Operators may adjust permitted consumer capacity only while preserving event ordering and downstream limits; blind replay is rejected because it can duplicate business processing.

sections.heading: Scope and interpretation
sections.text: The decision addresses backlog recovery, not a posting-order race inside the ledger. Deployment evidence and incident-specific recovery measurements remain separate records.

sections.heading: Business and service context
sections.text: Settlement and reporting follow payment acceptance through asynchronous processing stages. Each stage can complete at a different time, and a report can be accurate for its stated cutoff while omitting more recent work. Investigation therefore follows source identifiers through event consumption, reconciliation, and publication. Delay, mismatch, and accounting correction are separate observations. Combining them under a single label without tracing their respective records can conceal both the actual processing bottleneck and the required control response.

sections.text: Read the interface boundary and assumptions before applying the design to an incident. Compare the behavior described here with the configuration and procedure effective for the event under examination. Record which observations support the mechanism and which remain hypotheses. A design or accepted decision can explain intended behavior, but implementation and operating evidence must be inspected separately when the question concerns what actually occurred.

sections.heading: Application example
sections.text: During catch-up, a consumer can acknowledge rapidly while downstream reconciliation remains slow. That observation should trigger a check of where acknowledgement occurs and which work is still outstanding. It should not be interpreted as permission to raise the consumption limit indefinitely. The operator needs a view of event age and downstream completion for the same processing interval, with the original event references retained through any permitted retry or replay.

sections.heading: Design position
sections.text: DR acceptance now includes an explicit dependency inventory and a notification-path check. The recovery lead must trace customer-visible journeys beyond the restored database before recording an exercise as successful.

sections.heading: Supporting detail
sections.text: The inventory names event delivery, notification consumption, message preparation, and acknowledgement as separate checkpoints. An unresolved checkpoint is recorded as partial recovery, with an owner and follow-up action, instead of being hidden by an overall green infrastructure result.

sections.heading: Scope and interpretation
sections.text: This decision changes exercise acceptance. It does not certify a future failover or grant access to general regional health telemetry.

sections.heading: Business and service context
sections.text: Recovery is meaningful only when the required customer journey works across its dependencies. Infrastructure checks are necessary observations, but they do not automatically establish application completion. An exercise should retain both successful checkpoints and unresolved steps so a partial result remains intelligible. The tested scenario, execution date, and scope of evidence determine what can be concluded. Historical exercise results should not be presented as continuous assurance about present availability.

A design or accepted decision can explain intended behavior, but implementation and operating evidence must be inspected separately when the question concerns what actually occurred.

sections.heading: Application example
sections.text: A recovery review can show a restored database and a successful transaction read while the notification consumer still lacks a usable route. Record both results. The failed notification is not invalidated by the successful database check, and the database success need not be erased to explain the incomplete journey. This separation makes the corrective action specific: identify the omitted dependency, add its checkpoint, and require later execution evidence before accepting recovery.

sections.heading: Design position
sections.text: The operating-model decision separates original design authorship from ongoing service operation. Operational responsibility is to transfer through an approved handover, with documented escalation duties and acceptance of outstanding actions.

sections.heading: Supporting detail
sections.text: A handover includes runbook ownership, unresolved incident actions, access review, and catalog maintenance. Historical design records retain their original authorship so later investigators can distinguish who designed a component from who operates it in a subsequent period.

sections.heading: Scope and interpretation
sections.text: The decision defines the transfer method. The effective policy and handover minutes establish the dated transition; the live catalog is the authority for a current owner lookup.

sections.heading: Business and service context
sections.text: Design authorship, service accountability, and shift coverage are related but distinct responsibilities. A dated design can correctly name a team that is no longer responsible for day-to-day operation. A transfer record explains a change at its effective date, while a current directory resolves people and contact details. Retaining the original dates and attribution allows investigations to reconstruct responsibility without retroactively changing what an earlier reader would have known.

sections.heading: Application example
sections.text: Consider a design question raised after a handover. The engineer answering it may need the original team's rationale even though the new operating team owns the response action. Preserve both roles in the explanation. The handover packet should make unresolved work visible to the receiving team without rewriting the author field on old architecture. A useful transfer record therefore identifies what responsibility moved, when it moved, and which historical records still explain the design.

sections.heading: Design position
sections.text: Digital Payments Engineering is the design owner for MerchantConnect in this 2025 architecture baseline. The gateway separates merchant request handling from outbound PSP sessions so that downstream latency does not hold the customer interface indefinitely.

sections.heading: Supporting detail
sections.text: The design uses a pool of 200 outbound connections. Each request carries a merchant identifier and a correlation identifier; the correlation identifier supports investigation but does not establish an idempotency boundary.

sections.heading: Scope and interpretation

sections.heading: Application example
sections.text: In the baseline request path, the merchant-facing worker accepts an instruction, acquires an outbound session, and awaits the provider response. A lost acknowledgement can leave the caller uncertain even when the provider received the request. The design review should inspect session release and request correlation at that boundary before suggesting more inbound workers. This illustrative path describes the design assumptions; it is not a report that a particular incident or duplicate debit occurred during the baseline period.

sections.heading: Design position
sections.text: The digital payment journey separates checkout, merchant authorization, settlement, and reporting. PayFlow handles checkout interaction, MerchantConnect mediates PSP requests, and SettlementHub consumes events from EventMesh for downstream processing.

sections.heading: Supporting detail
sections.text: An accepted checkout response and a completed reconciliation are different milestones. Correlation identifiers let investigators follow the journey, while each service retains its own record of acceptance and completion. Reports must identify the processing cutoff they represent.

sections.heading: Scope and interpretation
sections.text: The map describes interfaces rather than an availability dashboard. A healthy response from one component cannot establish that every downstream consumer is up to date.

sections.text: Settlement and reporting follow payment acceptance through asynchronous processing stages. Each stage can complete at a different time, and a report can be accurate for its stated cutoff while omitting more recent work. Investigation therefore follows source identifiers through event consumption, reconciliation, and publication. Delay, mismatch, and accounting correction are separate observations. Combining them under a single label without tracing their respective records can conceal both the actual processing bottleneck and the required control response.

sections.heading: Application example
sections.text: For a payment appearing late in a corporate report, follow the original request reference into the settlement event and then the report cutoff. A successful checkout can be consistent with an earlier report cutoff. Conversely, a newly published report can still omit work that has not reconciled. The dependency map provides the route for that investigation, while the records at each stage establish what happened to the individual instruction being examined.

sections.heading: Design position
sections.text: Corporate limit enforcement uses the verified customer segment recorded by onboarding. The limit decision is evaluated before submission, and both the segment and the effective policy version are retained with the decision.

sections.heading: Supporting detail
sections.text: The limit service checks daily usage in the policy's accounting interval. A failed request must not silently change the customer's verification state. Support receives an explanation code distinguishing segment eligibility from exhaustion of the applicable allowance.

sections.heading: Scope and interpretation
sections.text: This document describes where the rule is enforced. The approved policy supplies the numerical threshold and effective date; architecture cannot independently widen a customer's allowance.

sections.heading: Business and service context
sections.text: Corporate payment eligibility, daily consumption, and operator permissions answer different questions. A customer can be eligible for an allowance while lacking enough remaining usage for a particular request. Equally, an authorized operator cannot change the corporate customer's segment simply by choosing another channel. Policy dates matter because a correct historical decision can differ from the rule applied later. Customer explanations must preserve the relevant segment, accounting interval, and effective version instead of quoting an isolated amount.

sections.heading: Design position
sections.text: FraudShield feature processing separates model inputs from customer-facing decline explanations. Detailed investigation can inspect velocity, session continuity, and beneficiary novelty, but those feature names are not customer instructions for obtaining approval.

sections.heading: Supporting detail
sections.text: Feature snapshots retain their extraction time and model release identifier. Reviewers compare like-for-like cohorts before attributing a change in decisions to a feature adjustment. Missing values are recorded explicitly instead of being silently interpreted as low risk.

sections.heading: Scope and interpretation
sections.text: Access to this architecture requires risk authorization. It describes the investigation surface without disclosing privileged rule configuration or declaring a quantified reduction in fraud losses.

sections.heading: Business and service context
sections.text: Payment review must balance customer friction with the need to examine uncertain activity. Customer-facing communication and internal investigation serve different purposes and have different access boundaries. A support reference helps an authorized reviewer find the underlying decision without exposing the features or controls used to make it. Observations must be interpreted within the relevant model and customer journey; a change in complaint descriptions alone does not establish the complete effect of a decision process.

sections.heading: Design position
sections.text: The privileged review architecture separates request creation, approval, grant application, and review evidence. A reviewer must not approve the same privileged grant that they requested, and the grant applier cannot erase the review history.

sections.heading: Supporting detail
sections.text: Grant records link the subject, resource, approver, and expiry. Review evidence is appended to an immutable audit stream with a stable record identifier. Revocation must update the grant state while retaining the prior decision for independent examination.

sections.heading: Scope and interpretation
sections.text: This restricted design specifies control boundaries. Installation of the workflow alone does not prove that operating reviews occurred or that an audit finding has been closed.

sections.heading: Business and service context
sections.text: Access-control assurance depends on a chain from requirement to implementation to demonstrated operation. A plan shows intended work; a release shows a mechanism was installed; review evidence shows what actually happened during an operating period. Each record has a different author and purpose. An auditor needs the relevant population and disposition history to assess coverage, while the action owner needs unresolved items to remain visible until their completion can be evidenced.

sections.heading: Application example
sections.text: A privileged account can remain technically usable after a reviewer decides that its justification has expired. sections.heading: Design position
sections.text: Payment failures use distinct diagnostic categories. MC_POOL_WAIT denotes outbound admission waiting, PF_DB_POOL_WAIT denotes a database connection wait, PSP_CONN_RESET denotes a closed upstream connection, and EM_CONSUMER_LAG denotes delayed event consumption.

sections.heading: Supporting detail
sections.text: A timeout describes an observed boundary, not a complete root cause. Record the service identifier, dependency, request phase, and timestamp before comparing an error with historical incidents. Preserve the original code even when summarizing it in business language.

sections.heading: Scope and interpretation
sections.text: Similar words such as pool, reset, and queue can refer to different resources. Matching a phrase without checking the affected component can produce an incorrect remediation choice.

sections.heading: Business and service context
sections.text: Payment enquiries can concern a present interruption, an earlier failure, or a customer-visible outcome. Those questions require different evidence. Service identifiers and timestamps help prevent a recent change note from being mistaken for a status report. A record of symptoms can guide investigation before a cause is established, while a completed postmortem explains the event it actually examined. Operational communication should preserve that difference when handing work between support, engineering, and incident coordination.

sections.heading: Application example
sections.text: When a support ticket says the pool is exhausted, ask which process emitted the code and which resource that process was waiting for. Database connections and provider sessions have different owners, lifetimes, and recovery paths. Attach the original diagnostic identifier to the translated symptom description so later searches can recover the distinction. This approach preserves useful wording variation without allowing a broad search match to become a root-cause conclusion on its own.

sections.heading: Design position
sections.text: The reviewed MerchantConnect capacity baseline has an outbound pool of 200 connections. Waiting work is held separately from active PSP sessions, so a queue increase does not demonstrate that the pool itself has expanded.

sections.heading: Supporting detail
sections.text: Configuration review captures the pool setting, worker concurrency, downstream timeout, and retry behavior together. A request to change one number must identify the pressure it is intended to relieve and the downstream capacity assumptions on which it depends.

sections.heading: Scope and interpretation

sections.heading: Business and service context
sections.text: An emergency response creates both an operational timeline and a governance timeline. The first records what was changed and whether service recovered. The second records authority, required review, and retained evidence. These timelines should remain linked without being collapsed into a single success flag. Urgency explains why an expedited path may be needed, but the responder must still preserve the evidence that allows a later reviewer to distinguish a permitted mitigation from an unrecorded exception.

sections.heading: Design position
sections.text: Investigation of MerchantConnect outbound starvation identifies unbounded concurrency and retry amplification as the repeated failure mechanism. More waiting requests generate additional attempts while slow PSP calls retain scarce sessions.

sections.heading: Supporting detail
sections.text: The review distinguishes the inbound work queue from the outbound client pool. Increasing pool capacity can postpone saturation, but it leaves the feedback loop intact and may move pressure to the PSP. Queue length, active sessions, and attempts per original request must be examined together.

sections.heading: Scope and interpretation
sections.text: This review recommends changing admission and retry behavior. It is technical evidence for a subsequent decision, not authorization to modify production configuration.

sections.heading: Business and service context
sections.text: Merchant payment processing crosses an outbound provider boundary. Waiting work, active connections, and client-visible responses describe different parts of that journey. A useful investigation preserves those distinctions and relates observations to the particular configuration and procedure in force. A temporary reduction in waiting work can be operationally useful without explaining why the original pressure accumulated. Service identity and observation time therefore remain essential when comparing records that use similar words for different failure modes.

sections.heading: Design position
sections.text: The duplicate-debit review finds that retry attempts crossed the MerchantConnect payment boundary without a merchant-scoped idempotency key. A timeout could therefore lead to a second execution instead of retrieval of the first execution's outcome.

sections.heading: Supporting detail
sections.text: A transport correlation identifier is unsuitable as a payment uniqueness guarantee: it can change between attempts. The review follows a request from merchant retry through settlement submission and identifies where the prior result must be durably associated with the original business operation.

sections.heading: Scope and interpretation
sections.text: The mechanism explains the reviewed July event. It does not establish that every retry-family incident involved duplicate debits, and the failed-attempt counter cannot be used as a duplicate-debit count.

sections.heading: Business and service context
sections.text: A payment operation can produce several network attempts. The commercial instruction, the transport attempt, and the settlement entry must remain distinguishable throughout investigation. An interrupted acknowledgement leaves uncertainty about the operation's result; it does not establish that repeating the request is harmless. Interface contracts and persistence boundaries determine what a retry means. Evidence should connect these boundaries through stable references before an analyst classifies an apparent duplicate or recommends further processing.

sections.heading: Design position
sections.text: SettlementHub consumes settlement events from EventMesh. Consumer lag can therefore postpone reconciliation even when a merchant-facing payment request has already completed. A campaign burst exposed this separation between request completion and downstream settlement progress.

sections.heading: Supporting detail
sections.text: The dependency crosses an asynchronous boundary. Increasing the request timeout does not drain the event backlog. Offsets, event age, reconciliation completion, and report publication must be inspected as separate observations along the same processing path.

sections.heading: Scope and interpretation
sections.text: This dependency explains how delay propagates. It does not make EventMesh lag equivalent to a LedgerCore posting-order race, which requires a separate causal investigation.

sections.heading: Business and service context
sections.text: Settlement and reporting follow payment acceptance through asynchronous processing stages. Each stage can complete at a different time, and a report can be accurate for its stated cutoff while omitting more recent work. Investigation therefore follows source identifiers through event consumption, reconciliation, and publication. Delay, mismatch, and accounting correction are separate observations. Combining them under a single label without tracing their respective records can conceal both the actual processing bottleneck and the required control response.

sections.heading: Scope and interpretation

sections.heading: Business and service context

The tested scenario, execution date, and scope of evidence determine what can be concluded. Historical exercise results should not be presented as continuous assurance about present availability.

sections.heading: Scope and interpretation
sections.text: This record establishes the rollout action. The policy remains the authority for eligibility and amounts; a deployment record does not independently authorize a different limit.

sections.heading: Business and service context
sections.text: Corporate payment eligibility, daily consumption, and operator permissions answer different questions. Policy dates matter because a correct historical decision can differ from the rule applied later. Customer explanations must preserve the relevant segment, accounting interval, and effective version instead of quoting an isolated amount.

sections.heading: Observed failure and confirmed mechanism
sections.text: SettlementHub consumer lag accumulated behind an EventMesh event burst. Accepted payment work reached downstream reconciliation later than expected.

sections.heading: Impact and measurement boundary
sections.text: The attributable interruption lasted 22 minutes, from 2025-10-02T09:00:00Z to 2025-10-02T09:22:00Z. The service recorded 6,400 failed or rejected attempts. This is an attempt count, not unique payments or customers: one business instruction can generate several attempts. Unique customer impact and exact currency loss were not recorded. No assumed transaction value has been attached to the attempt count.

sections.heading: Response and recovery
sections.text: Operators compared event timestamps with committed consumer position, paced recovery to the downstream reconciliation path, and retained the delayed event references. The handover retained observation times and the original service and operation references. Responders separated uncertain outcomes from confirmed failures so that recovery did not silently convert pending work into successful or lost payments.

sections.heading: Interpretation limits
sections.text: A payment's acceptance time and appearance in a report are different milestones. This event does not establish a ledger posting-order defect.

sections.heading: Operational context
sections.text: Settlement and reporting follow payment acceptance through asynchronous processing stages. Each stage can complete at a different time, and a report can be accurate for its stated cutoff while omitting more recent work. Investigation therefore follows source identifiers through event consumption, reconciliation, and publication. Delay, mismatch, and accounting correction are separate observations. Combining them under a single label without tracing their respective records can conceal both the actual processing bottleneck and the required control response.

sections.heading: Observed failure and confirmed mechanism
sections.text: A PSP Gateway routing deployment directed authorization traffic through an unavailable network path. Requests failed before a usable provider response could return.

sections.heading: Impact and measurement boundary
sections.text: The attributable interruption lasted 36 minutes, from 2026-05-31T09:00:00Z to 2026-05-31T09:36:00Z. The service recorded 7,300 failed or rejected attempts. This is an attempt count, not unique payments or customers: one business instruction can generate several attempts. Unique customer impact and exact currency loss were not recorded. No assumed transaction value has been attached to the attempt count.

sections.heading: Response and recovery
sections.text: The response compared route configuration with the preceding baseline, reverted the routing change, and confirmed successful connections before reopening ordinary admission. The handover retained observation times and the original service and operation references. Responders separated uncertain outcomes from confirmed failures so that recovery did not silently convert pending work into successful or lost payments.

sections.heading: Change assessment and follow-up
sections.text: The investigation links the event to preceding change CHG-210. The mechanism above explains the relation; the timing is not the sole basis for attribution. Recovery observations, the initiating mechanism, and longer-term remediation are retained as separate parts of the record. A proposed follow-up remains a proposal until its own decision and implementation evidence exists.

sections.heading: Interpretation limits
sections.text: The change relation is supported by route evidence. It does not establish provider-side degradation or a failure of the idempotency contract.

sections.heading: Operational context
sections.text: Payment enquiries can concern a present interruption, an earlier failure, or a customer-visible outcome. Those questions require different evidence. Service identifiers and timestamps help prevent a recent change note from being mistaken for a status report. A record of symptoms can guide investigation before a cause is established, while a completed postmortem explains the event it actually examined. Operational communication should preserve that difference when handing work between support, engineering, and incident coordination.

sections.text: DataGateway resolver timeouts interrupted its own upstream lookup path. DG_DNS_TIMEOUT described name resolution rather than occupied MerchantConnect PSP sessions.

sections.heading: Impact and measurement boundary
sections.text: The attributable interruption lasted 16 minutes, from 2026-08-02T09:00:00Z to 2026-08-02T09:16:00Z. A failed-payment attempt total was not measured for this adjacent-service event. Unique customer impact and exact currency loss are also unrecorded. The absence of a measurement is represented as unknown, not as evidence of zero impact. sections.heading: Response and recovery
sections.text: Responders verified resolver behavior, restored the lookup path, and retained the affected service identity with the original error observations. The handover retained observation times and the original service and operation references. Responders separated uncertain outcomes from confirmed failures so that recovery did not silently convert pending work into successful or lost payments.

sections.heading: Change assessment and follow-up
sections.text: The investigation does not classify this event as change-related. That classification does not imply that the service had never been deployed or modified; it describes the evidence for this particular interruption. sections.heading: Interpretation limits
sections.text: This event is unrelated to MerchantConnect capacity recurrence. The existence of a dependency relationship is insufficient to assert that the same incident propagated into payments.

sections.heading: Operational context
sections.text: Payment enquiries can concern a present interruption, an earlier failure, or a customer-visible outcome. Those questions require different evidence. Service identifiers and timestamps help prevent a recent change note from being mistaken for a status report. A record of symptoms can guide investigation before a cause is established, while a completed postmortem explains the event it actually examined. Operational communication should preserve that difference when handing work between support, engineering, and incident coordination.

sections.heading: Request acceptance
sections.text:
Record what the checkout response actually establishes. Acceptance means the request entered processing; completion requires a business outcome. Preserve the support reference when an acknowledgement is interrupted so later investigation can distinguish a pending instruction from a fresh submission.

Related authority: [PROD-001 — PayFlow checkout journey](DOC-PROD-001.md#section-01), version 1, published 2025-07-18. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Outbound connection boundary
sections.text:
Separate waiting work from active PSP sessions. An increase in acquisition waits can occur while inbound workers remain healthy. Capture the effective connection setting with the observation rather than inferring it from a queue graph or a remembered baseline.

Related authority: [ARCH-007 — MerchantConnect capacity configuration](DOC-ARCH-007.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-06-19. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Retry amplification
sections.text:
Compare attempts per original request with active connections and waiting work. Repeated attempts can intensify the same pressure that produced the original timeout. Increasing a resource limit without examining this feedback path can move the bottleneck to another dependency.

Related authority: [ARCHREV-004 — MerchantConnect retry amplification review](DOC-ARCHREV-004.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-06-25. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Admission behavior
sections.text:
Admission control decides whether additional work can enter the constrained path. Inspect what happens to deferred or rejected requests as well as accepted traffic. A smaller internal queue is not necessarily recovery if work disappeared without an attributable customer outcome.

Related authority: [ADR-021 — Bounded concurrency and back pressure decision](DOC-ADR-021.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-07-02. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Back pressure signals
sections.text:
Follow pressure signals from the outbound boundary to the caller. Confirm that upstream work observes the signal instead of immediately retrying. Retain request identifiers across deferral so a bounded queue does not become a source of ambiguous payment outcomes.

Related authority: [RB-003-v2 — MerchantConnect revised saturation response](DOC-RB-003-v2.md#section-01), version 2, published 2026-07-16. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Circuit state
sections.text:
A circuit protects an unhealthy dependency by suppressing calls under the accepted design. Investigate why it opened and what evidence permits another attempt. Treat circuit behavior and provider recovery as separate observations; an open circuit is not itself the provider's root cause.

Related authority: [ADR-021 — Bounded concurrency and back pressure decision](DOC-ADR-021.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-07-02. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Retry budgets
sections.text:
Check whether repeated attempts consume a bounded allowance associated with the operation. Worker movement must not silently reset the budget. Preserve the original key and outcome reference so a client cannot create apparently fresh work merely by changing transport details.

Related authority: [PROD-007 — Merchant retry guidance](DOC-PROD-007.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-07-31. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Temporary capacity mitigation
sections.text:
A tuning release can improve waiting behavior without removing the underlying feedback mechanism. Preserve its actual configuration scope when comparing later events. Do not describe every temporary adjustment as the subsequent architectural redesign or assume that a completed change closed all recurrence actions.

Related authority: [CHG-139 — MerchantConnect pool tuning](DOC-CHG-139.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-03-28. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Material change review
sections.text:
Compute the proposed increase against the documented baseline and consult the effective approval rule. Record downstream assumptions and rollback conditions. The existence of spare local resources does not establish that the external provider can safely absorb more simultaneous requests.

Related authority: [POL-007-v2 — Material capacity change standard](DOC-POL-007-v2.md#section-01), version 2, published 2026-06-01. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Emergency evidence packet
sections.text:
Keep the incident qualification, requested action, authority, implementation time, and recovery evidence distinguishable. A clear packet allows reviewers to assess urgency and compliance independently. Contacting the responsible person is only a communication step; retain the actual approval decision separately.

Related authority: [RB-010 — Emergency capacity change procedure](DOC-RB-010.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-06-03. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Merchant operation identity
sections.text:
Associate a retry with the merchant's business operation rather than the process that happened to send it. Preserve the key through interrupted acknowledgements. A replacement worker must find the persisted outcome instead of treating its first local observation as a new payment.

Related authority: [PROD-006-v2 — Merchant retry API current spec](DOC-PROD-006-v2.md#section-01), version 2, published 2026-07-30. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Conflicting key reuse
sections.text:
Compare the normalized payload when a key already exists. A different amount or destination must not inherit a previous successful result or silently start a new debit. Retain the explicit conflict outcome so support can explain why the request was rejected.

Related authority: [ADR-024 — Replay safe payments decision](DOC-ADR-024.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-07-28. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Replay-safe settlement
sections.text:
Trace uniqueness through settlement submission, not only the merchant-facing endpoint. An interface-level deduplication check is incomplete if another worker can independently submit the same business operation downstream. Retain the settlement reference beside the operation result for reconciliation.

Related authority: [ADR-024 — Replay safe payments decision](DOC-ADR-024.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-07-28. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Ambiguous acknowledgements
sections.text:
An interrupted acknowledgement leaves an uncertainty to resolve. Check persisted payment and settlement outcomes before replay. Generating a new key to escape the uncertainty can create a second business instruction and should not be described as ordinary transport recovery.

Related authority: [RB-004 — Duplicate payment triage](DOC-RB-004.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-07-30. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Duplicate investigation units
sections.text:
Maintain separate counts for transport attempts, commercial instructions, and executed debits. A failed-attempt metric can include rejected work and repeated attempts. It therefore cannot be relabeled as a count of duplicate debits without examining the business-level evidence.

Related authority: [ARCHREV-006 — Duplicate debit boundary review](DOC-ARCHREV-006.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-07-24. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Historical interface versions
sections.text:
When investigating an older client, identify the contract effective for that client and event date. Do not silently apply a later mandatory-key promise to an earlier interface. Versioned specifications explain what behavior was expected at each point in the history.

Related authority: [PROD-006-v1 — Merchant retry API prior spec](DOC-PROD-006-v1.md#section-01), version 1, published 2025-07-18. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Release correlation
sections.text:
A deployment timestamp is a useful investigation boundary, but temporal proximity is not sufficient causal evidence. Compare the changed path with the incident's observed mechanism. Preserve release chronology even when a later review supplies a more complete explanation.

Related authority: [CHG-118 — Retry redesign release](DOC-CHG-118.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-07-19. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Post-fix observation
sections.text:
Retain later retry events with their individual mechanisms. A family label is useful for discovery but too broad to establish recurrence of one defect. Compare operation identity, persisted outcomes, and affected boundaries before deciding that a fix failed.

Related authority: [ARCHREV-014 — Idempotency follow up review](DOC-ARCHREV-014.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-08-28. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Event production and consumption
sections.text:
Payment acceptance and settlement consumption cross an asynchronous boundary. Track the producer reference and consumer position independently. A successful synchronous response can coexist with downstream delay without either observation being false.

Related authority: [ARCH-002 — Digital payment dependency map](DOC-ARCH-002.md#section-01), version 1, published 2025-07-15. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Backlog age
sections.text:
Measure the age of unprocessed events as well as the number waiting. A queue can shrink because work moved, expired, or was discarded. Recovery evidence should show processing and acknowledgement, not only a lower count in a dashboard.

Related authority: [RB-008-v2 — EventMesh revised backlog response](DOC-RB-008-v2.md#section-01), version 2, published 2026-06-02. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Consumer partition progress
sections.text:
Inspect the delayed subscription or partition rather than relying only on process availability. A running consumer group may conceal one stalled path. Record the last committed position with the observation time so another responder can verify actual progress.

Related authority: [RB-005 — Settlement lag response](DOC-RB-005.md#section-01), version 1, published 2025-07-25. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Controlled catch-up
sections.text:
A recovery burst can overwhelm the next service even if the event consumer has spare capacity. Pace catch-up against downstream processing limits and preserve ordering. Reconciliation must confirm that accelerated consumption did not create a new ambiguity.

Related authority: [ADR-025 — Event consumer backpressure decision](DOC-ADR-025.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-05-28. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Reconciliation cutoff
sections.text:
A reconciliation result describes work completed through a specified cutoff. Retain outstanding references beyond that boundary and explain their disposition separately. Do not advance the cutoff solely because an upstream producer has resumed normal operation.

Related authority: [POL-012 — Settlement reconciliation standard](DOC-POL-012.md#section-01), version 1, published 2025-07-01. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Corporate report freshness
sections.text:
Explain the difference between report publication and the latest payment included. A newly opened report can still reflect an earlier processing cutoff. Customer support should preserve the report reference and cutoff when investigating missing recent activity.

Related authority: [PROD-009 — Corporate reconciliation report spec](DOC-PROD-009.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-05-25. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Ledger race separation
sections.text:
Use the existence of a ledger-control reference as a reason to seek authorized evidence, not to infer its contents. Event backlog and posting order are different investigative paths. An operations handbook must not reproduce confidential accounting-adjustment evidence for an unauthorized reader.

Related authority: [ARCHREV-008 — EventMesh settlement dependency review](DOC-ARCHREV-008.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-05-22. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Database pool diagnostics
sections.text:
A database acquisition wait and an outbound HTTP pool wait can share a symptom while requiring different checks. Identify the resource and owning service before applying a runbook. Preserve original error codes alongside any plain-language summary.

Related authority: [ARCH-006 — Payment error taxonomy](DOC-ARCH-006.md#section-01), version 1, published 2025-07-20. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Provider resets
sections.text:
A reset identifies an interrupted connection boundary. It does not by itself show that local sessions were exhausted or that the provider's internal cause is known. Retain the connection phase and request outcome uncertainty during classification.

Related authority: [ARCH-006 — Payment error taxonomy](DOC-ARCH-006.md#section-01), version 1, published 2025-07-20. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: DNS before connection
sections.text:
Resolution occurs before a new outbound session can be established. Confirm whether the endpoint was resolved before attributing failure to pool capacity. Existing healthy sessions may coexist with failures to create new ones when resolution is impaired.

Related authority: [ARCH-006 — Payment error taxonomy](DOC-ARCH-006.md#section-01), version 1, published 2025-07-20. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Trust failures
sections.text:
Certificate validation failure is different from an unavailable connection slot. Record the trust error and connection stage without disabling validation as an assumed remedy. The incident's approved recovery evidence, rather than the shared word timeout, determines classification.

Related authority: [ARCH-006 — Payment error taxonomy](DOC-ARCH-006.md#section-01), version 1, published 2025-07-20. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Service-specific attribution
sections.text:
Assign the incident to the service whose interruption is recorded. A downstream dependency named in its explanation does not automatically create a second incident. Preserve cross-service consequences without duplicating the same event in a collection analysis.

Related authority: [ARCH-002 — Digital payment dependency map](DOC-ARCH-002.md#section-01), version 1, published 2025-07-15. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Incident identity
sections.text:
Use the incident identifier to reconcile a report, change reference, and compendium entry. Multiple documents can describe one event. Keep separate source citations while preserving one event identity for any later calculation over incident records.

Related authority: [ARCH-006 — Payment error taxonomy](DOC-ARCH-006.md#section-01), version 1, published 2025-07-20. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Interruption duration
sections.text:
Read the start and end of the attributable interruption rather than substituting ticket-open time. The reporting purpose determines whether recovery observation or administrative closure matters. An unresolved financial item can remain after an operational interruption ends.

Related authority: [POL-012 — Settlement reconciliation standard](DOC-POL-012.md#section-01), version 1, published 2025-07-01. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Unknown customer impact
sections.text:
A failed attempt does not identify a unique customer. Repeated attempts and shared corporate operators can make those units diverge substantially. Preserve unknown customer counts explicitly and avoid translating attempt totals into customer totals without additional evidence.

Related authority: [PROD-005 — Settlement report delivery contract](DOC-PROD-005.md#section-01), version 1, published 2025-07-18. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Financial-loss limits
sections.text:
Delayed reporting and failed attempts can create concern without establishing a measured loss. A monetary assessment needs its own recorded amounts and methodology. Do not introduce an assumed average payment value to make an incomplete operational metric appear financially precise.

Related authority: [PROD-009 — Corporate reconciliation report spec](DOC-PROD-009.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-05-25. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Observation windows
sections.text:
State the periods being compared and retain qualifying residual incidents. Unequal exposure windows and missing traffic denominators limit the interpretation of a before-and-after comparison. The reports support observation; they do not independently supply a controlled causal experiment.

Related authority: [ARCHREV-013 — Post rollout capacity load review](DOC-ARCHREV-013.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-08-28. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Source effective dates
sections.text:
Publication, effective date, and event date answer different questions. A policy may be published before it takes effect, while a report may be written after the event. Select the rule applicable to the action rather than simply the newest file.

Related authority: [POL-007-v2 — Material capacity change standard](DOC-POL-007-v2.md#section-01), version 2, published 2026-06-01. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Current status boundary
sections.text:
Historical documents explain completed events and procedures. A present incident enquiry needs a current operational record with an update time. If that record is unavailable, preserve uncertainty instead of substituting a recent release note as a status report.

Related authority: [RB-009 — Payment live triage](DOC-RB-009.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-08-20. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Escalation identity
sections.text:
Resolve whether the request concerns an owner, incident commander, manager, or shift responder. Those roles can be held by different people. Use the appropriate dated or current authority before requesting contact details, and retain the service identifier through the lookup.

Related authority: [RB-013 — Service ownership escalation guide](DOC-RB-013.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-07-02. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Customer-visible uncertainty
sections.text:
Support should distinguish pending confirmation from confirmed failure or completion. A transport error alone may leave the business result unresolved. Preserve the original support reference so the customer is not encouraged to submit duplicate instructions to discover the outcome.

Related authority: [PROD-001 — PayFlow checkout journey](DOC-PROD-001.md#section-01), version 1, published 2025-07-18. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Safe incident handover
sections.text:
Transfer observed symptoms, attempted actions, preserved references, and unresolved hypotheses together. The next responder should know which boundary was checked and which remains uncertain. A handover that only says fixed or still broken loses the evidence needed to continue investigation.

Related authority: [RB-003-v2 — MerchantConnect revised saturation response](DOC-RB-003-v2.md#section-01), version 2, published 2026-07-16. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Decision scope
sections.text:
Begin a control review by naming the decision being assessed and its effective period. A policy recommendation, approved rule, and implemented setting are different records. Preserve their sequence so a reviewer can see whether the required authority existed when the action occurred.

Related authority: [POL-019 — Corporate limit review cadence](DOC-POL-019.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-03-27. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Corporate segment evidence
sections.text:
A segment-based allowance depends on verified eligibility. Retain the evidence establishing that status and distinguish it from a customer's desire for a higher limit. Product demand can motivate a review without supplying the eligibility evidence needed for a particular customer.

Related authority: [RISK-003 — Corporate limit regulatory review](DOC-RISK-003.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-03-10. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Shared daily usage
sections.text:
Examine whether usage is shared across operators and channels for the corporate customer. Testing only a single user can miss a bypass at the account boundary. Preserve the accounting interval and policy version alongside the resulting limit decision.

Related authority: [ARCH-003 — Corporate limit enforcement design](DOC-ARCH-003.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-03-25. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Committee conditions
sections.text:
Read conditional approval together with its outstanding requirements. A committee's support for a proposal does not mean every prerequisite has been satisfied. Track the policy and implementation records that convert the decision into an operative customer rule.

Related authority: [MTG-003 — Corporate limit risk committee](DOC-MTG-003.md#section-01), version 1, published 2026-03-20. Use the referenced record's effective interval and stated scope when applying this section.

sections.heading: Policy supersession
sections.text:
Retain the prior version and the replacement's effective boundary. Historical decisions need the version in force at the time. A present search result should not erase evidence that a different allowance legitimately applied earlier.
